lesson_title: Two Coins and the Rule of Gears
hook_text: Roll two coins together and you have just discovered the first law of gears.
clip_script: Put two coins flat on a desk, edges touching. Roll one clockwise. The other one rolls anticlockwise. Every time. Gears are just coins with teeth so they cannot slip, and that means two meshing gears always turn opposite ways. Driver clockwise, driven anticlockwise. Add a third gear in a row and it is clockwise again. The direction flips at every tooth-to-tooth meeting. So what if you need the last gear to turn the same way as the first? Drop a gear in the middle. That is the idler. Two flips cancel and the ends match. The idler changes nothing else, not the speed, not the force, just the direction, and because it rubs on both sides it wears fastest, so engineers make it from harder metal. Two coins. One rule. Every gearbox on Earth.
visual_style: Two whiteboard coins rolling with curved arrows; they grow teeth and become gears; a third gear slides between them and the arrows on the outer two switch to match.
pacing: Coin demonstration, the rule, the idler fix, the one-line takeaway.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw a three-gear train with the right arrows on each.
